items.title: A Concrete Definition of “Product Sense” (and How to Build It)
items.summary: Product sense means predicting which product decisions will succeed based on patterns learned through experimentation — and knowing when those patterns apply.

items.title: 4 Mistakes to Avoid When Presenting Complex UX Maps
items.summary: UX maps clarify complexity but are often presented poorly. Prepare audiences by communicating early, speaking plainly, and focusing on collaborative outcomes.

items.title: Design-System Maturity: A 6-Dimension Framework
items.summary: Use this maturity model to assess your design system’s health and identify where to focus next.

items.title: What are Design Specs?
items.summary: When designs get rejected in dev review, missing specs are often the culprit. A solid spec covers layout, interactions, requirements, and project scope.

items.title: Quantity Yields Quality in UX: Iterative vs. Parallel vs. Competitive Design
items.summary: No design is perfect on the first try. Combining iteration, parallel design, and competitive testing helps teams move quickly, explore broadly, and make confident, evidence-based design decisions.

items.title: Atomic Research: Small Insights, Big Impact
items.summary: Atomic research breaks user research into small, evidence-backed units to improve analysis, repository organization, and cross-team collaboration.

items.title: Closing the Loop: What to Do After a Design Critique Ends
items.summary: Most designers invest in running critiques but skip the followup. That missing step is often why feedback culture breaks down.

items.title: The Case for Design Disposables
items.summary: Design disposables are rough artifacts you make to think, not to deliver. Learn to tell them apart from deliverables and avoid the sunk-cost trap.

items.title: Small by Design: The Strength of Lean Design-System Teams
items.summary: Lean design-system teams, when strategically planned, can move faster, prioritize sharply, and scale impact beyond their size.

items.title: Boost Design Autonomy with an Information Pipeline
items.summary: A four-step framework for building influence over product direction by closing the information gaps that large, complex organizations create.

items.title: Field Guide to Explaining UX Strategy
items.summary: Simple, relatable ways to explain complex UX strategy concepts like UX vision, goals, OKRs, and outcomes. Translate UX strategy into language anyone on your team can understand.

items.title: Design Process Isn't Dead, It’s Compressed
items.summary: As AI speeds up design work, the argument to "throw out the process" misrepresents how experienced designers work.

items.title: Project Postmortems for UX Teams: Learning from Success and Failure
items.summary: Although postmortems are one of the most powerful learning tools in product development, most teams haven't yet discovered how to use them effectively.

items.title: Your Design System Needs an Enforcer
items.summary: Although design systems promise consistency, most still fail without someone actively enforcing the rules and making teams follow them.

items.title: Prompt to Design Interfaces: Why Vague Prompts Fail and How to Fix Them
items.summary: Create better AI-prototyping designs by using precise visual keywords, references, analysis, as well as mock data and code snippets.

items.title: When is High-fidelity Worth It?
items.summary: 4 questions to ask yourself when deciding whether process work should be high-fidelity or not.

items.title: Good from Afar, But Far from Good: AI Prototyping in Real Design Contexts
items.summary: AI prototyping tools follow general directions but lack the judgment and nuance of an experienced designer.

items.title: From Confrontation to Collaboration: The Developer-Designer Relationship
items.summary: The infamous developer-designer relationship doesn’t need to be toxic. Design and development teams should approach collaboration as coowners of the product experience.

items.title: AI-Assisted Prototyping: Promise and Pitfalls
items.summary: AI tools turn static designs into working prototypes fast, but speed can mask flaws. Use them to explore, not as a final product.

items.title: Template Trap
items.summary: Templates help, but only when used with intent. Use them thoughtfully, adapt them to context, and don’t skip the critical thinking.
